Two things happened in this pass:

Fixed a real bug. I'd claimed Cyrillic and Greek were "already covered by Bebas Neue" — checked that claim and it was wrong. The free Google Fonts build of Bebas Neue is Latin-only; Cyrillic support only exists in the paid "Bebas Neue Pro." So Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Greek, and any other Cyrillic/Greek content would have silently rendered as tofu boxes on title cards. Now routed to Inter (already loaded, full coverage) whenever detected.

Expanded from 22 to 46 mapped scripts, adding real living-language coverage beyond India: Tibetan, Mongolian (traditional), Thaana (Maldives), the Indonesian regional scripts (Javanese, Balinese, Sundanese, Batak, Buginese), Southeast Asian minority scripts (Tai Viet, New Tai Lue, Cham), Middle Eastern (Syriac), and a meaningful set of African scripts — Adlam (Fulani, ~40M speakers), N'Ko (Manding languages), Tifinagh (Amazigh/Berber, ~30M speakers) — plus Cherokee, Canadian Aboriginal syllabics, Yi, and Bopomofo.

What's still out: purely historical/liturgical scripts with no living content-creation use case (Runic, Linear B, Egyptian hieroglyphs, etc.) — deliberately excluded since there's no realistic scenario where someone's pasting a script in those. If you ever hit a real gap, the pattern's simple to extend — a Unicode range and a font name, same as everything above.

does this include europian languages too?

Claude responded: Yes — European languages are actually the best-covered category, split two ways:

Thought for 10s
Thought for 10s

Yes — European languages are actually the best-covered category, split two ways:

Latin-alphabet languages (English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Romanian, Nordic languages, Baltic languages, Turkish, Basque, Catalan, Welsh, Irish, etc.) — these needed zero extra work. Inter and Bebas Neue already have full Latin Extended support, so all those accented/diacritic characters (é, ñ, ü, ø, å, ł, š, ő, ç...) just render correctly out of the box, no dynamic font loading triggered at all.

Cyrillic and Greek (Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Belarusian, Macedonian, Greek) — these are exactly what I just fixed. Bebas Neue's free version turned out to be Latin-only, so before this fix, titles in those languages would've shown blank boxes. Now they correctly fall back to Inter.

One honest caveat on that: for Infographic bullets and Title/End cards, Cyrillic/Greek text will render in Inter Bold rather than the condensed Bebas Neue marquee style, since Bebas Neue genuinely can't draw those glyphs — no font can fake that. So the poster look is slightly different for those languages specifically, everything else (Latin-script European languages) keeps the full marquee aesthetic since Bebas Neue handles them natively.

So combined: yes, every European language is covered, either natively or via fallback.

You said: so basically, as long as someone gives the script in their language we give them the output in their language

so basically, as long as someone gives the script in their language we give them the output in their language

Claude responded: Yes — that's the accurate way to describe it, with one honest boundary worth being precise about, since "give them the output in their language" could be read …

Yes — that's the accurate way to describe it, with one honest boundary worth being precise about, since "give them the output in their language" could be read two ways:

What's true: If someone pastes a script/prompt in their language — Tamil, Russian, Arabic, French, Swahili, whatever — the tool will render that exact text correctly on screen: title cards, infographic slides, bullet points, all in their language, with the right script rendering instead of blank boxes. That part is genuinely automatic, no setup needed.

What's NOT happening: the tool doesn't translate anything. If you paste an English script, you get English output. If you paste a Tamil script, you get Tamil output — but only because you gave it Tamil to begin with. There's no "give it English, get it in Hindi" conversion; it's not a translation engine, it's a faithful-rendering engine. The only place actual translation exists is the small en/ta/hi dropdown for the app's own buttons and menus (which I hand-wrote), and that's separate from your content entirely.

So the honest one-line version: whatever language you write your script or prompt in, that's the language your slides come out in — not "give it any language and pick your output language," but "your input language becomes your output language, correctly rendered."

Claude responded: Yes, absolutely — nothing about hosting it on GitHub locks it in place.

Yes, absolutely — nothing about hosting it on GitHub locks it in place. It's just a static file sitting in a repo; you (or I, guiding you) can update it any time.

The workflow going forward is simple: whenever you want a change, tell me here, I'll edit the file the same way I have been, hand you the updated index.html, and you re-upload it to the same FrameatWork repo — GitHub lets you overwrite the existing file directly from the "Add file → Upload files" screen, same as last time. Commit it, wait a minute for Pages to redeploy, refresh your live URL, done.

A couple of things worth knowing about that flow:

  • Each upload is a new commit, so GitHub keeps every past version — if a change ever breaks something, you can roll back to an earlier commit from the repo's history.
  • There's no build step or deployment pipeline to manage since it's one HTML file — no risk of a broken deploy blocking you.
  • If you ever want it smoother than manual re-uploads (e.g., editing occasionally becomes frequent), GitHub also lets you edit the file directly in the browser via the pencil/edit icon on the file page — useful for tiny tweaks, though for anything substantial you'd still want to come back here so I can test it properly first like I've been doing.

So: yes, it's very much a living file, not a one-time export.

Claude responded: Depends on what device you're on:

Thought for 2s
Thought for 2s

Depends on what device you're on:

On desktop (Chrome/Edge/Safari):

  1. Tap the file card I shared above (the one labeled frameworks).
  2. Your browser will either open it in a new tab or prompt a download — if it opens in a tab, use File → Save Page As (or Ctrl+S / Cmd+S) and save it.
  3. Make sure it saves as frameworks.html (or rename it to index.html right there, saves you a step later).

On mobile (phone/tablet):

  1. Tap the file card.
  2. Depending on your browser, you'll get a "Download" option or a share sheet — choose Download or Save to Files/Downloads.
  3. It'll land in your device's Downloads or Files app as frameworks.html.

Either way, once it's on your device:

  • Go to your FrameatWork GitHub repo → Add file → Upload files.
  • Drag in the saved file (or tap to browse and select it).
  • If it's still named frameworks.html, rename it to index.html in that same upload screen before committing — GitHub Pages looks for index.html specifically.
  • Commit the change, wait a minute, refresh your live URL.

If tapping the card doesn't trigger a download at all on your setup, let me know what happens when you tap it (opens raw code in a new tab? nothing happens? asks to choose an app?) and I'll adjust the instructions to match.
